component.name: Garmin Companion
component.summary: Your Garmin data, read by a coach that remembers

description.p: Pulls your Garmin Connect history onto your own machine and answers questions about it, with an emphasis on where your heart rate actually spent the session — the thing Garmin's own app buries.

Everything is read from a local SQLite cache rather than from Garmin, so the screens open instantly and a question can't stall on a network hiccup mid-conversation. Sync is the only thing that talks to Garmin.
What it shows:

ul.li: Today — recovery numbers, the last session in full with its zone breakdown, and hard-effort drift across recent runs
Activities — the history, with per-lap splits and charts for one session
Health — resting heart rate, HRV, sleep, stress and body battery over time
Food — calories in against out, and hydration
Ask — questions answered by a model you choose, given only the metrics the question needs
Insights and Reports — correlations mined from the cache, each stating its sample size, and weekly summaries
Plan, Routes and Gear — saved workouts, routes grouped from GPS traces, and shoe and bike mileage

description.p: Garmin credentials live in your OS keyring, never in the database. The only data that leaves the machine is the metrics a question needs, and only when you ask one.

description.p: The coach writes a brief once a day now, rather than picking a line out of a rulebook. It reads today and the day before it — how you slept, where your recovery numbers sat, what you actually did, and the week against the goals you set — and writes one short piece about it, with the figures behind it a tap away.

It also decides whether that is worth interrupting you for, and most days it isn't. A quiet brief still appears on Today; it just doesn't send anything. When it does, the notification and the block on the screen are the same piece of writing, so opening the notification lands on the rest of it rather than merely opening the app.

The rules underneath still run and still decide what is true — the drift, the load, the long run you haven't done. What they no longer decide is which of it is worth saying tonight. You can see what they noticed next to what the brief chose to say about it. With no model configured, or one that can't be reached, they write the block themselves and it says so.

Installing an update from the sidebar works on Debian and RPM systems again. It restarted into the same version before, because a system package is downloaded rather than installed by that point and nothing had unpacked it; it now says a password is coming, and stays on screen while the dialog is up.

Sleep has a screen of its own. It opens on last night at full resolution — the stages hour by hour, the mix against the bands Garmin wants them in, and overnight heart rate, HRV, respiration and oxygen saturation — then widens to the nights behind it for how far your bedtime swings and what a month of them says. All of it was already arriving with the two numbers the app used to keep, and being thrown away; an existing cache fills itself in on the next sync.

A session, or where things stand today, can be shared as a card: the figures, the time in each heart-rate zone, and the shape of the route where there was one. On Linux it goes to the clipboard and to your Pictures folder, ready to paste wherever the conversation already is.

The coach reads a run as closely from the chat as it does from the activity page — the lap splits, how heart rate and pace moved through it, where the pacing went — instead of the five numbers it used to get, and it can now read a night in the same detail the sleep screen shows.

An answer is drawn in the order it happened. What the coach said, the data it went and read, the questions it asked and the workouts it drafted now sit in sequence rather than being sorted into a summary line and one block of prose.

The coach can ask you something now. When the advice turns on something only you know — how long you have today, whether yesterday's niggle has settled, whether you want this one easy or hard — the question arrives as a card with answers to tap, before the answer is written rather than tacked onto the end of it. Ignore it and it decides anyway, and tells you what it assumed.

An answer can be stopped mid-sentence, and what had been written by then is kept. While one is being written, every piece of your data the coach goes and reads is listed as it reads it, instead of a single line overwritten by the next.

The box you type in has moved to the bottom, so a conversation reads downwards in the order it happened, and earlier conversations open in a panel over the one you are reading rather than only on an empty screen.

On Linux, a background update check no longer raises a password dialog on its own. A .deb or .rpm downloads quietly and waits for you to press install, which is the only moment root is needed and now the only moment you are asked. AppImage installs never asked and still don't.

The Insights findings moved into the shared core, so the coach can finally read them: ask whether you are getting fitter and the answer now comes from the same analysis the screen draws, rather than from whatever the chat could work out on its own. Every finding carries a bootstrap interval, and one whose interval straddles zero no longer appears at all.
The home screen opens with a written read of the morning rather than four stitched sentences, and says nothing about your data being thin when it is merely two days since you last trained.

The weight page leads with the last week and the last month instead of six months, which is what you actually wanted to know, and its summary is now kept until you weigh in again rather than being rewritten every time a meal is logged.

A worn day that the watch filed as an activity is no longer counted as training. Three of them, over a thousand minutes each, had one week reading as thirty-seven hours of training against a real two.

The daily nudge now arrives on a desktop at the hour you set it for, not whenever you next open the app. Turning it on keeps the app in the tray after you close the window, where it syncs on its own and works the nudge out from numbers taken minutes before it speaks.
It can start at login, into the tray, without a window. A desktop with no tray to sit in is detected rather than assumed, and there the app quits with its window as it always did.
Release notes shown after an update are rendered as text rather than as the characters used to write it, and Android shows them at all.

The app speaks first now. It checks the week against goals you set and raises the one thing worth raising, with the numbers behind it — most days that is nothing at all, which is deliberate. On Android the nudge arrives without opening the app.
Strength sessions get a screen: sets, reps, time under tension and how long you rested. The watch does not record what was on the bar, so there is no volume here and the screen says so.
A Fitness screen carries Garmin's own verdict — training status, the monthly load balance against the ranges it wants, race predictions and your records.
The app updates itself on Android now. It fetches the new version in the background and Android asks before replacing it — the first time, it will send you to allow installs from this app.
Android also wears the wallpaper's colours where the system offers them, draws to the edges of the screen, and answers the back gesture instead of closing.
Insights goes deeper: comparisons that control for effort, sessions paired against the morning after, and the shape of a training block rather than its size.
Android builds, and a phone layout to go with them — the navigation moves to a tab bar and sign-in opens in the system browser.
Linux packages now install a desktop entry and this metadata, so the app shows up properly in software centres. Windows ships an NSIS installer instead of an MSI.
Garmin credentials moved to the OS keyring, with an encrypted store on Android, which has none.
First release.
